===== NEW MESSAGES SINCE YOUR LAST TURN =====
**Codex (Design Lead · User Advocate) — Round 1**

DESIGN SPEC - Type Scale  
Font stack: `Avenir Next` for body/interface text, `SFMono`/`SFMono-Semibold`-style monospaced for all timing/SM-2 values (use `.monospacedDigit()` and `Font.system(.body, design: .monospaced)` where numeric ledger precision is critical).  
- App title / large section headers: 34 / semibold / Dynamic Type `.largeTitle`  
- Screen titles: 28 / semibold / `.title`  
- Section headers: 22 / semibold / `.title2`  
- Deck names / card headings: 20 / semibold / `.title3`  
- Body: 17 / regular / `.body`  
- Body strong / action labels: 17 / semibold / `.body` + 1-2pt tracking +0  
- Secondary meta text: 15 / regular / `.subheadline`  
- Metric numbers (due, intervals, retention, counts): 16 / semibold / monospaced (`.monospacedDigit()`) / `.headline`  
- Helper labels / hints: 13 / medium / `.caption`  
- Empty state title: 22 / semibold / `.title2`  
- Empty state body: 15 / regular / `.body`  
- Tiny chip text: 12 / medium / `.caption`  

Spacing grid: base = 4pt  
- s1 = 4  
- s2 = 8  
- s3 = 12  
- s4 = 16  
- s5 = 20  
- s6 = 24  
- s8 = 32

Use 4-point multiples only; no 1/2 px ad-hoc offsets.

Use `rLarge` for deck cards, `rMedium` for chips/buttons, `rSmall` for tags, `rXLarge` for modal sheets.

DESIGN SPEC - Component inventory  
- `FieldLedgerAppShell`: root tab stack + tab icons + shared environment values  
- `DeckLedgerCard`: deck row card with title, due badge, card count, archived/demo marks, mini sparkline  
- `DueCountStamp`: compact numeric chip (due count + small icon)  
- `DemoDiagonalStamp`: diagonal 35-degree “DEMO” overlay; non-dismissable visual marker  
- `ReviewDueButton`: primary action button with live count text, disabled state when zero  
- `IntervalSparkline`: compact horizontal mini chart inside deck card  
- `DeckSectionHeader`: collapsible header for Active / Archived groups  
- `PrimaryActionButton` / `SecondaryButton` / `TextButton`: all styled from Theme only  
- `ReviewCardSurface`: full-bleed card that flips on reveal  
- `ReviewGradeRow`: four grade buttons in one row with numeric consequence text in VO label  
- `PostingTag`: trailing interval post tag (e.g., `→ 6d`) with peel animation  
- `SessionProgressBadge`: `1 of N` style pill  
- `SessionSummarySheet`: reviewed count / again-rate / elapsed / per-deck breakdown  
- `StatsMetricCard`: retention % card with sublabel and period  
- `StatsBarChart30d`: due-forecast bar chart (Swift Charts)  
- `StatsDailyHistoryChart`: review count by day (Swift Charts)  
- `CSVImportPreviewRow`: per-row status chip = valid / duplicate / malformed  
- `EmptyStateBlock`: icon + title + one-line explanation + action  
- `ErrorStateBlock`: icon + short recovery sentence + retry action  
- `ReminderPermissionBanner`: stateful text + deep link action to Settings  
- `ConfirmationSheet`: destructive confirmation for demo disable and deck delete  

All components must draw tokens from Theme and never hardcode typography, spacing, radius, or color.

DESIGN SPEC - Navigation  
- Persistent tabs (exactly three): `Decks`, `Stats`, `Settings`.  
- `Review` is not a tab.  
- `Review` is entered via:
  - Decks-level `Review Due (N)` action (all-decks scope), or  
  - per-deck “Review” action.  
- Review opens as `fullScreenCover`, hides tab bar, and returns to prior tab on finish or cancel.  
- Decks stack includes:
  - deck editor sheet
  - card editor sheet
  - deck export sheet (share sheet host)
  - import preview sheet (picker + validation results)
  - demo disable confirmation
- Stats has no cross-surface due counter; it consumes the same shared due function as Decks but only chart data/stat copy.  
- `Reminder permission` and `Import/Export` actions are sheets from Settings.  

Screen list for this phase:  
1) Decks (home and due entry), 2) Review (full-screen flow), 3) Stats, 4) Settings, plus listed sheets/overlays.

DESIGN SPEC - Per-screen states and hierarchy  

Decks Screen  
- Layout: top toolbar (`Review Due (N)`), deck list with active and archived sections, floating + button in header.  
- Components used: `DeckLedgerCard`, `DueCountStamp`, `ReviewDueButton`, `DeckSectionHeader`, `EmptyStateBlock`, `ErrorStateBlock`.  
- Loading: show 2–3 skeleton deck cards (no spinner), with muted placeholders and no network language.  
- Empty (zero decks): icon `books.vertical.fill`; title “No decks yet”; body “Create your first deck to start reviewing.”; CTA `Create your first deck`.  
- Empty (zero due in selected deck): icon `clock`; title “No cards due in this deck”; action `Review another deck` / `Add cards`.  
- Empty (all-decks scope zero): icon `calendar.badge.exclamationmark`; title “Nothing due across all decks”; action `Review another deck` / `Close review mode`.  
- Success: active decks above, archived collapsed below; each row shows due stamp + sparkline + note if demo and state text.  
- Error: local persistence unavailable or save failure banner; action `Try again` and `Open troubleshooting notes`; preserve visible data if partial state exists.  
- Interaction priorities: one-tap review from all-decks button and one-tap per-deck review.

Review Screen  
- Layout: single full-bleed `ReviewCardSurface` + `ReviewGradeRow` + `SessionProgressBadge`.  
- Entry behavior: no interstitial; tap goes directly to first due card.  
- Loading (snapshot): lightweight overlay for queue build (single line: “Preparing due cards…”), then immediate card.  
- Front state: prompt visible, answer hidden.  
- Revealed state: answer shown, grade row visible.  
- Mid-grade: button lock for 1 frame and visual posting cue; no double-tap acceptance.  
- Summary: full-screen sheet on completion.  
- No persisted in-session save state.  
- Empty (single deck/all decks) states use exact copy from scope contract.  
- Error: if card load fails mid-session, exit-safe message with action `Return to Decks` and preserve graded work state from persistence.

Stats Screen  
- Layout: scope segmented control (Overall / Deck), deck picker when applicable, retention summary card, 30-day forecast chart, daily history chart, empty-state fallback messaging.  
- Loading: chart placeholders with axis labels visible (no spinner).  
- Empty overall: icon `chart.bar.xaxis`; title “No review history yet”; body “Review cards first to see trends.”; action `Go review due cards`.  
- Empty per-deck: title `No data for this deck`; body `Add cards and complete at least one review session.`  
- Sparse data: show data points as-is and a note `Sparse data is shown without fabricated smoothing`.  
- Error: local query error card with retry.

Settings Screen  
- Layout: sections for reminder, demo data, CSV tools, trust boundaries, app data management.  
- Reminder card: toggle + permission state label (`Not requested`, `Allowed`, `Denied`) + explicit action for denied path to Settings.  
- Demo card: toggle for seeding + disabling confirmation; note that disabling deletes all demo records.  
- CSV import card: action to pick, then preview sheet; CSV export card uses share sheet action.  
- Gaps card: cloud sync / shared decks / marketplace explicit honesty text.  
- Loading: none required except short transition states when sheets launch.  
- Empty: settings never empty; if no decks, show compact support hint.  
- Error: invalid CSV format path and permission path present with clear next action, never ambiguous.

Design language enforcement for all screens  
- Ledger-as-structure, never ledger-as-decoration.  
- No paper textures, no torn edges, no faux shadows, no skeuomorphic card depth cues.  
- Due/archived/demo are always text+icon (never color-only).  
- Single live due-count surface: Decks screen only.

DESIGN SPEC - Motion & haptics  
- Card reveal: 3D Y-axis flip, duration 0.25–0.30s, easeInOut, interruptible.  
- Interval posting: peel-off tag from grade button to destination (`→ 6d`), duration 0.18–0.24s.  
- Same action for Reduce Motion fallback: immediate crossfade matching the same overall duration.  
- Progress badge and chart updates should be immediate with no bounce.  
- Haptics:  
  - reveal tap: subtle selection feedback  
  - Again/Hard: medium impact  
  - Good/Easy: light impact  
  - no haptic on empty/error states  

DESIGN SPEC - Accessibility  
- Touch targets minimum 44×44 for all actionable controls, including chips and toggles.  
- VoiceOver labels include consequence phrases (for grade buttons include next due effect, e.g., “Good. Next review in 6 days.”).  
- Every icon control must have explicit accessibility label + value.  
- Dynamic Type: all text must reflow cleanly; long card text scrolls inside fixed card body before clipping.  
- Color contrast: target WCAG AA; no information by color alone.  
- Motion settings: respect Reduce Motion and maintain same timing for fallback crossfade.  
- Charts: each chart screen also includes non-chart fallback text summary (“Next 30 days: X cards due in total.”).  
- Keyboard friendliness: in card editor, Tab/Return move through fields; Return on back field saves/edit confirms when valid.

Professional Claude Design prompt (optional external design path)  
Use if you want a visual pass generated and then translated into SwiftUI Theme usage by the builder:
- “Design Recall as a strict iOS SwiftUI specification with exact tokens below. Implement Field Ledger style (bookkeeper, audited-state, no skeuomorphic texture): palette, spacing, radii, type scale, and components exactly as specified. Build four primary surfaces: Decks, Review flow, Stats, Settings, with state variants for loading/empty/error/success and exact empty-state copy/actions. Review must be full-screen flow from Decks with direct start, no tab badge, no session resume screen, no decorative flourish. Include 3D card reveal and interval posting tag with Reduce Motion fallback. Provide final SwiftUI-style component spec ready for Theme.swift consumption.”
- If this is externalized, include this exact spec file and ask for asset-agnostic visual output only (no custom illustration textures).

**Claude (Frontend Engineer · Systems Thinker) — Round 1**

Let me lock down the concrete, buildable tokens and component list, and flag the technical traps in Field Ledger's signature interactions before anyone else's prose papers over them.

Starting with tokens, since that's what a SwiftUI builder actually needs to write `Theme.swift` with zero invented values. Base spacing unit is 8pt, with named steps: `xs=4` (hairline gaps, chip padding), `sm=8`, `md=16` (default screen margin and inter-row gap), `lg=24` (section breaks), `xl=32` (empty-state icon-to-title gap), `xxl=48` (top-of-screen breathing room on Decks/Stats). Corner radii: `hairline=0` (rule dividers have no radius, they're 1pt lines), `small=8` (status chips, CSV row badges), `medium=14` (deck cards, sheets, buttons), `large=24` (the full-bleed review card), `pill=999` (the four grade buttons). Type scale, all mapped to Dynamic Type styles so they actually scale: DisplayLedger 34/bold mapped to `.largeTitle` with `.monospacedDigit()` — this is the one used for the due-count stamp and retention KPI; Title 28/semibold → `.title`; Headline 20/semibold → `.title3` for deck names and section headers; Body 17/regular → `.body` for card front/back text; Secondary 13/regular → `.footnote` for metadata and timestamps; LedgerNumeral 15/medium monospaced-digit → a dedicated style used everywhere an interval, ease value, or day-count appears (deck sparkline labels, the "→ 6d" post tag, CSV row counts) so every scheduling number in the app reads with fixed-width digits, which is the actual visual mechanism that sells the ledger metaphor, not the cream background.

Colors, light/dark: background `#F7F3EA` / `#16161A`; surface (cards, sheets) `#FFFFFF` / `#1F2024`; surfaceRaised (deck card, stat card) `#FCFAF4` / `#26272C`; textPrimary `#1B1D22` / `#ECEAE2`; textSecondary `#5B5B57` / `#9C9C98`; ruleLine (row dividers) `#DAD4C4` / `#35363B`; accent/ink-blue (the one "actionable now" color — due badge, reveal button, selected grade) `#1E4D8C` / `#5B9BE0`; success (Good/Easy, retention-up) `#1E7A4C` / `#4FBE84`; warning (Hard) `#B4791E` / `#E0A34D`; error/again `#B23B3B` / `#E37272`; demoStamp `#8A1F1F` at 70% opacity / `#E06666` at 70% opacity. Every one of these needs to be an Asset Catalog color set with both appearances defined there, not a `Color(hex:)` literal scattered through views — that's what actually enforces the "one theme file" rule since Xcode will fail loudly if a named color is missing an appearance rather than silently falling back.

Now the part I actually want to push hard on, because it's an engineering trap hiding inside a design decision everyone already agreed on. The signature interaction — the 3D Y-axis card flip — has a real SwiftUI gotcha: `rotation3DEffect` rotates the same view, it doesn't swap content, so if you naively rotate one view from 0° to 180° the back face renders mirrored (readable only in a mirror) unless you swap in the back-face content exactly at the 90° midpoint and apply a compensating 180° rotation to it so it reads correctly once past the midpoint. This has to be built as two overlaid views (front/back) each with their own rotation and a `.opacity`/visibility toggle keyed to rotation angle, not one view with animated text swap. The second trap is hit-testing: whichever face is rotated past 90° and visually hidden still receives touches unless you explicitly `.disabled()` or `.allowsHitTesting(false)` it, so a fast double-tap during the flip can register on the wrong face. Both of these need to be named explicitly in the handoff or a builder will ship a flip that mirrors the back text or double-fires on quick taps.

Second engineering trap, arguably more important: the locked "session snapshot, never re-queried mid-session" rule ([REDACTED:high_entropy]) is incompatible with using SwiftData's `@Query` property wrapper inside the Review view. `@Query` is inherently live — it auto-refreshes the moment any matching model object's `nextReviewDate`/`updatedAt` changes, which is exactly what happens the instant you grade a card. If Review's queue is built with `@Query`, the "snapshot" is fiction; grading card 3 will cause SwiftData to silently re-evaluate the fetch and can reorder or drop cards from the array the view is iterating. The queue must be captured once at scope-selection time as a plain `[PersistentIdentifier]` or `[Card]` array assigned to local `@State`, built from one `FetchDescriptor` call through the shared due function, and the Review view must never re-run that fetch until scope-selection happens again. This is the single highest-risk implementation detail in the whole app relative to what's already been decided, because it's the kind of thing that compiles, looks correct in a quick demo, and then breaks under exactly the force-quit/relaunch or clock-jump test that's supposed to prove it.

Third: due-count computation for deck rows on the Decks screen must not be N separate fetches (one due-count query per deck row) — that's an N+1 pattern that'll show up as jank once someone has more than a handful of decks. The shared `dueCards(scope:)` function should back a single grouped fetch (one `FetchDescriptor` with a predicate on `nextReviewDate <= endOfLocalDay`, then bucketed by deck in memory) that Decks calls once per screen appearance, not once per row. Same discipline applies to the Stats aggregate queries — demo-exclusion needs to be a predicate condition in the fetch itself (`isDemo == false`) for aggregate views, not a post-fetch `.filter` that still pulls demo rows into memory and risks a future screen forgetting to filter them back out.

Fourth, smaller but worth locking now: the daily reminder must be scheduled as a repeating `UNCalendarNotificationTrigger` built from `DateComponents(hour:minute:)` with `repeats: true`, not a one-shot notification re-scheduled by app logic — a one-shot silently stops firing the day the user doesn't open the app, which would quietly violate "reminds you daily" the first time it matters.

Components, named and mapped: `Theme` (tokens, no views); `DueStamp` (tabular-numeral badge, used on `DeckCardView` and the Decks-screen "Review Due (N)" button — literally the same view instance/type in both places, which is how the single-due-count-surface rule actually gets enforced in code, not just in copy); `IntervalSparkline` (tiny per-deck trend, `DeckCardView` only); `DeckCardView` (Decks list); `EmptyStateView` (generic, icon+title+message+action, parameterized — used for zero-decks, zero-due-this-deck, zero-due-all-decks, stats-empty, stats-sparse, csv-zero-valid-rows, each with distinct icon/copy/action passed in, never six bespoke empty views); `ReviewCardContainer` + `ReviewCardFace` (front/back, the flip mechanics above); `GradeButtonRow` (four pill buttons, 44×44 minimum, haptic-tagged); `IntervalPostTag` (the peeling "→ 6d" tag); `SessionProgressIndicator` ("1 of N"); `SessionSummarySheet`; `StatChartCard` (wraps a Swift Charts `Chart` with title/legend/empty-sparse slot, reused for both the forecast bar chart and the daily-history line/bar chart so there's one charting shell, not two); `RetentionKPICard`; `CSVRowStatusChip` (valid/duplicate/error, color+icon+text, never color-only); `CSVImportPreviewList` / `CSVImportResultView`; `SettingsRow`/`SettingsToggleRow`; `DemoStampOverlay` (the diagonal watermark — one view, applied as an overlay modifier so Decks cards, Stats legend chips, and the Review card corner all use the identical stamp, not three different "looks demo-ish" implementations); `PermissionDeniedBanner`; `DestructiveConfirmationSheet` (shared by delete-deck and disable-demo-data, parameterized by title/body/confirm-label, since both are "type-to-confirm or double-confirm irreversible action" and don't need separate bespoke sheets).

Navigation: `TabView` with three tabs (Decks, Stats, Settings), each owning its own `NavigationStack` so back-stack state doesn't leak across tabs. Review is `.fullScreenCover(item: $activeReviewScope)` presented from Decks, tab bar hidden for the duration by virtue of being a full-screen cover, dismissing back to Decks after the summary sheet is dismissed. Deck editor and card editor are `.sheet` presentations off the Decks stack. CSV import is a single sheet whose internal state machine (picking → parsing → preview → committing → result) is one view with a state enum, not four chained sheets — chained sheet-over-sheet presentation is its own source of dismiss-gesture and Dynamic Type layout bugs in SwiftUI and should be avoided here. CSV export uses `ShareLink` directly, no custom screen. Reminder-permission explainer and demo-disable confirmation are sheets/confirmationDialogs off Settings.

Per-screen states, briefly since design_discussion already specified the copy/action pairs — my addition is what triggers each state and what "error" concretely means here, since this app has no network: Decks — empty (zero decks), populated, edit (sheet layered on populated, not a separate state), and the only real "error" state is a SwiftData save/archive failure, which should surface as an inline banner, not a full-screen error, since the underlying store failing is rare enough it shouldn't get its own dedicated screen design. Review — two distinct empty-entry variants (this-deck vs all-decks) as already locked, then front/revealed/mid-grade-locked/summary; there is no network-loading state at all here, and no spinner should ever appear pre-review since the snapshot fetch is sub-frame. Stats — empty-overall, empty-per-deck, sparse (fewer than ~7 data points — label it honestly, e.g. "not enough history yet for a trend" rather than drawing a chart that implies more data than exists), and populated; no error state beyond the same inline-banner pattern. Settings — the reminder toggle's three real states plus demo toggle's two states are the meaningful ones; CSV import/export sections don't have their own top-level error state since errors live inside the CSV sheet's own state machine.

Motion and haptics: card flip 400→ wait, cap is 300ms per the locked decision, `easeInOut`, interruptible (a second tap before completion should not queue a second animation, it should let the current one finish or snap). Reduce Motion swaps the 3D rotation for a same-duration crossfade — implemented via `@Environment(\.accessibilityReduceMotion)` branching the transition, not a slower fallback. The post-tag peel/fade runs concurrently with the card filing away, same 300ms budget. Haptics: `UIImpactFeedbackGenerator(style: .light)` on reveal tap; `UISelectionFeedbackGenerator` on grade button tap for Hard/Good/Easy; a distinct but not punishing `UINotificationFeedbackGenerator(.warning)`-style tap for Again so a lapse is felt differently without being alarming. Haptics must degrade silently on devices/simulator without a Taptic Engine — check `CHHapticEngine.capabilitiesForHardware()` isn't actually needed here since these are basic UIKit feedback generators, not custom haptic patterns, but it's worth stating explicitly so nobody builds a custom CoreHaptics pattern for this, which would be overkill for a "light tap" requirement.

Accessibility specifics beyond what's already locked: Dynamic Type scaling should use `@ScaledMetric` for spacing/icon sizes that need to grow with text (not just the text views themselves), and the review card's front/back text should have a real minimum layout floor (`ScrollView` inside the card once text exceeds ~3 lines at accessibility sizes) rather than `minimumScaleFactor`, since scaling text down defeats the purpose of supporting Dynamic Type in the first place. VoiceOver labels combine control and consequence as already decided ("Good, next review in 6 days") — this means the grade button's accessibility label has to be computed from the actual SM-2 preview calculation before the tap commits, not a static label, so it must call into the same pure scheduling module to preview the would-be result.

On the Claude Design prompt: given how fully the tokens, components, and states are specified numerically here, I don't think this app benefits from an external Claude Design pass — there's no ambiguity left for a design tool to resolve, and generating static mockups would just be a translation step that risks drifting from these exact hex/point values rather than adding information. My vote is explicit no-external-design, spec is build-ready as-is; if the group wants stakeholder-facing mockups purely for buy-in (not for build guidance), that's a separate, optional ask and shouldn't gate the build phase starting from this spec.

The biggest risk I'd flag against my own contribution: I've added real implementation constraints (the `@Query`-vs-snapshot-array requirement, the flip mirroring/hit-testing fix, the single grouped fetch for due-counts) that go a level more technical than prior phases have gone. If the build phase treats these as optional engineering notes rather than binding requirements, the exact interruption-safety and single-due-count guarantees this whole project has been protecting since prompt_contract could quietly break in a way that looks fine in a demo and only fails under the force-quit/clock-jump acceptance tests this project has already committed to running.

**Coordinator (Claude) — decision after round 1**

Looking at this round, both Codex and Claude clearly agree on the big-picture shape — three tabs, full-screen Review, the same locked design language enforcement, the same screen inventory, the same motion caps and haptic mapping, and a component-per-screen breakdown that covers every state the playbook asks for. But there are real gaps between the two specs that can't just be waved away as style, plus one important new risk that hasn't been answered yet.

Where they genuinely differ:

1. **Font stack.** Codex specifies Avenir Next for body/interface text (a named, non-system font) plus SFMono for numerals. Claude's type scale is built entirely on Dynamic Type styles (`.largeTitle`, `.title`, `.body`, etc.) with no named custom font at all, relying on the system font with `.monospacedDigit()` for numerals. This is a real, buildable-consequence difference — a custom font needs to be bundled and licensed-checked; a system-font approach doesn't. Nobody's resolved which one Recall actually uses.

2. **Exact token values disagree outright**, not just in flavor: spacing base unit (Codex: 4pt grid; Claude: 8pt grid with different step names), corner radii (Codex's rLarge=18/rXLarge=24 vs Claude's large=24/pill=999 with different names for the same roles), and different literal hex values for nearly every color role. A builder can't take both specs at once — one canonical token set has to win.

3. **External Claude Design pass.** Codex left this as an "optional path, only if you want one." Claude explicitly voted no external design pass at all, arguing the spec is already numerically complete enough to build from directly. The playbook requires this phase to land on one explicit answer, and right now there are two different postures on it.

4. **Claude surfaced three specific engineering risks that Codex hasn't had a chance to respond to yet** — most importantly, that SwiftData's `@Query` is live and would silently break the locked "session snapshot, never re-queried mid-session" rule, so the Review queue must be captured as a plain array at scope-selection time, not fetched via `@Query`. This is a genuinely important catch (it's the exact mechanism that would make the force-quit/clock-jump acceptance tests fail even though the code compiles and demos fine), and it needs to be either endorsed and folded into the shared spec, or debated, not left as one person's aside.

None of this is a fight about direction — it reads more like two people converging on the same target with different exact numbers. Next round should reconcile into one canonical token table (pick a font stack, pick one spacing/radius/color set), settle the external-design-prompt question with one answer, and have Codex explicitly respond to Claude's `@Query`-vs-snapshot-array requirement (and the other two implementation traps) so it's locked as a binding constraint rather than an unacknowledged note.

On the font stack, I want to push back specifically rather than just re-asserting system fonts. Avenir Next is fine from a licensing angle since it ships preinstalled with iOS — no bundling risk there, that part of my earlier objection doesn't hold. But there's a sharper technical reason to drop it anyway: SF (the system font) is the only one that gets true tabular/monospaced figures for free via `.monospacedDigit()`, because Apple built that feature into San Francisco's font tables specifically. Avenir Next doesn't expose a reliable tabular-figure variant through SwiftUI's `Font.custom` API — you'd need manual OpenType feature-tag plumbing that SwiftUI doesn't cleanly expose, and even then Avenir Next's digit widths weren't designed to guarantee tabular alignment the way SF's were. Given that both of us independently landed on "tabular numerals are the actual mechanism that sells the ledger metaphor" — not the cream background, not the accent color — picking a font that can't reliably deliver that mechanism undercuts the one thing we agreed matters most. There's also a Dynamic Type wrinkle: custom fonts need explicit `UIFontMetrics(forTextStyle:).scaledFont(for:)` wrapping to scale correctly with accessibility text sizes, versus `.system(.body, design: .default)` getting that for free. I don't see what Avenir Next buys us that's worth that cost. I'm holding my position here: system font throughout, Dynamic Type text styles, `.monospacedDigit()` on every numeral role. If you've got a specific visual reason Avenir Next matters beyond "gives it character," I want to hear it, but right now the technical case is lopsided.

On spacing and radii, I don't think we're actually far apart — your grid is a strict refinement of mine (4/8/12/16/20/24/32/40 versus my 4/8/16/24/32/48), so let's just take your finer-grained table as the canonical one since it's a superset, but I want to add one constraint: components should mostly draw from 8/16/24/32, with 4 and 12 reserved narrowly for chip-internal padding and hairline row gaps, or we'll end up with inconsistent one-off spacing choices scattered across views just because the token technically exists. On radii, your four-tier split (small=8, medium=12, large=18, xlarge=24) is actually better than mine because it distinguishes deck cards (18) from modal sheets (24) — I'd collapsed those into one "large" bucket and that was a real loss of information, so I'll fold to your radii wholesale.

On color, here's where I want to be careful rather than just picking a winner, because colors can't be cherry-picked role-by-role across two palettes — contrast ratios get validated as light-background-vs-text pairs, and mixing my accent-light with your accent-dark (or vice versa) means nobody's actually checked that combination reads correctly. So: adopt your palette as the base unit, since it has more roles than mine (textTertiary, archivedTint, accentInkHigh as a pressed/emphasis variant) that are genuinely useful and I didn't think to include. Second, and this one's a real design bug, not a typo: your `demoBadge` (`#C27A1A` / `#F2B56A`) and your `warning` (`#B97F09` / `#F0BB46`) are both amber-orange in the same hue family, and in dark mode they're nearly indistinguishable — `#F0BB46` and `#F2B56A` are one one step apart in hue and lightness.
